title: the one at every doorway
hookLine: why Hindus begin everything with Ganesha, and the tusk he broke to keep writing

cards: Every Hindu beginning starts with him, so this one does too. A small statue on a taxi dashboard. A picture above a shop counter.
His name printed at the top of a wedding invitation, before anyone else's. Elephant head, round belly, one tusk broken. He sits wherever things start, and that's the clue to who he is.

teach.b: Start with the name. Ganesha is gana plus isha: lord of the ganas, the attendants of the god Shiva. His best-known title is Vighnaharta.
Vighna, an obstacle; harta, one who removes. The remover of obstacles.
This is why Hindus begin everything with Ganesha: before a wedding, a puja, a new shop, a new home or an exam, you honor first the one who clears the way. And there's a story about him and a page.
When the sage Vyasa was ready to give the world the Mahabharata, he needed a scribe who could keep up.
Ganesha agreed, on one condition: Vyasa must never stop. Vyasa added his own: Ganesha must understand every verse before he wrote it down.

So whenever Vyasa needed time, he spoke a verse so knotted that even Ganesha had to stop and think. And one telling says that when Ganesha's pen gave out, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing.
That's the broken tusk in his pictures. The remover of obstacles is also a god of wisdom and learning.
So some people write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before they begin. Namah means a bow: a bow to Ganesha, before the work.

how: Hindus honor Ganesha first at pujas, weddings, housewarmings and new beginnings, keep his image near doorways and in shops, print his image or name at the top of invitations, and some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before starting to write.

games.q: nani's moving in with us saturday!! dad's making a card for the welcome puja and ganesha's on top AGAIN. sam asked why he's always first. wait, why??
o: he's Vighnaharta, the remover of obstacles. hindus honor him before anything begins, so the road is clear.
he's the god of good luck, so he's basically a lucky charm on the card.
he's the most important god, so he outranks everyone else.
games.why: Ganesha is Vighnaharta, the remover of obstacles, so Hindus honor him before every beginning. Nani moving in is a big beginning, so he goes first on the card.

games.q: who he is — tap the pairs.
p: a bow to Ganesha, before the work

s: it means lord of the ganas, the attendants of Shiva.
Ganesha is honored first, before a beginning
as Vighnaharta, the remover of obstacles, he's invoked at the start of ceremonies, weddings and new work.
the namah in shri ganeshaya namah is the same bow as in namaste
namah, namas: a bow. day one's word, hiding in day six.

games.q: a family is opening a new shop tomorrow morning. in the custom this lesson describes, what comes before the first sale?
o: unlock the shutters and start selling.
honor Ganesha, the remover of obstacles.
wait for the first customer to walk in.
games.why: beginnings start with Vighnaharta: clear the road, then begin.

games.q: build his title: obstacle + one who removes.

practice: One breath with the bell. Think of something you're beginning this week. If you pray, say shri ganeshaya namah once, under your breath, the way many Hindus do before they start.
If you don't, rest a hand on the door or the notebook, and name what's in the way. Then breathe out, and begin.

wordCard.voice: Ganesha. Lord of the ganas, remover of obstacles, the one at the door. First word on your strand, and the first name.

orig.note: Sanskrit: gana, the attendants, plus isha, lord. lord of the ganas.

carryVoice: Your line: clear the road, then begin. It's why his name comes first on so many invitations, and why he came first here. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 1 (Ganesha as scribe for Vyasa)
